Chris has spent twenty years advancing surf lifesaving at the national level, and Australian lifesavers train, patrol and resuscitate differently because of it. His national service began at the 2006 SLSA Youth Development Forum and has continued without pause ever since: fourteen years on the Lifesaving Members Advisory Committee (2012-2025), nine of them as National Chair of Lifesaving (2016-2025), alongside twelve years on the National Meritorious Awards Committee, which he chaired from 2017 to 2024.

As National Chair he reshaped how every Australian lifesaver is trained. He chaired the 2019 National Lifesaving Curriculum Review, chaired the rewrite of the Public Safety and Aquatic Rescue manual and produced its first online interactive edition, built the first nationally delivered blended learning model for the Surf Rescue Certificate and Bronze Medallion, and chaired three national course redesigns (Bronze Medallion, Silver Medallion Aquatic Rescue and Silver Medallion Patrol Captain). That body of work earned an international award for best use of blended learning in 2020.

He then looked to the future. He founded and facilitated SLSA's inaugural National Innovation Day (2024), founded and chaired the Expanding Horizons Review (2024), and served as National Implementation Lead for Lifesaving CPR (2024-2026), the first nationally coordinated CPR quality improvement initiative implemented by a community first aid organisation in Australia, personally leading the national roadshow that upskilled trainers around the country.

His contribution is conspicuous as well as distinguished. He was named SLSA Australian Surf Lifesaver of the Year in 2011/12, the youngest ever recipient and the only Tasmanian recipient, and holds the International Life Saving Federation Citation of Merit. Through all of it he has remained a frontline volunteer, patrolling every season since 2004 across Ulverstone and Elouera SLSCs, and his output is so far beyond what members expect of a volunteer that he is routinely mistaken for paid staff. Few members in the modern era have a contribution that is so national, so sustained and so directly attributable to one person.
EOF

Chris's club service is distinguished by leadership and education rather than tenure alone. He has patrolled for 22 unbroken seasons since joining Ulverstone SLSC in 2004, and he patrols still, now at Elouera SLSC in Sydney while remaining a continuing member of his home club. Sustained frontline service across two clubs and two states, without a single season's break, is itself uncommon; what makes it distinguished is what he built along the way.

As Patrol Captain for nine consecutive seasons (2007-2016) he carried frontline rescue responsibility on Ulverstone's beach. As Vice President, Lifesaving (2011) and Club Training Officer (2011-2013) he built the club's lifesaving operations and education capability, and from 2007 he has served continuously as a Trainer, Assessor and Facilitator, delivering award courses that began at club level and grew to branch, state and national delivery. These club roles were the foundation of everything that followed: the training systems he later rebuilt nationally were first learned, tested and taught on his own club's beach.

His peers recognised it twice, naming him Club Person of the Year in 2010/11 and again in 2011/12, back-to-back recognition across consecutive seasons. Beyond the formal roles, Chris remains the member every club officer knows they can call. He always takes the phone call, gives the advice, or helps with the project or problem in front of them, and he has done so for two decades.
EOF

At branch level Chris has consistently held the roles that carry real operational accountability for members and the public. As a Senior Duty Officer with SLS Sydney (2022-present) he is one of the people responsible for coordinating the branch's emergency lifesaving response, and he has served on the SLS Sydney Support Operations Team since 2020. That role builds directly on his earlier work in Tasmania, where he helped establish the Duty Officer function itself, authoring the training and standards the role still runs on.

His branch service began as Secretary of Tasmania's Regional Lifesaving Committee (2010-2012), and he has continued to assist at branch and regional level in every state he has lived in. That pattern is what makes his service significant: Chris is one of the few members who has carried operational lifesaving responsibility at club, branch, state and national level simultaneously, which means the national policy he writes is informed by the beach, and the branch operations he coordinates are informed by national direction. It has allowed him to roll out national policy and direction effectively while remaining genuinely involved at every level of the organisation, and it has been sustained for more than fifteen years across two states.
EOF

Chris's state service is distinguished by both its depth and the fact that it spans three states, with peer-judged excellence in every domain he has touched. In Tasmania he progressed from State Development Squad Captain (2005/06) and Under-19 Surf Life Saver of the Year (2007) through thirteen years on the State Emergency Response Team (2007-2020), the Awards of Excellence Panel (2009-2016), State Patrol Assessor (2010-2016) and State Duty Officer (2014-2020), to Chair of Lifesaving (2012-2016), the state's senior lifesaving position, before stepping up to the national chair. As state Chair he authored Tasmania's Duty Officer training and standards and chaired the editorial panel that produced SLST's inaugural Standard Operating Procedures, documents the state's operations still stand on.

His signature state contribution is the Lifesaving Development Camp. He coordinated Tasmania's inaugural camp and ran it for six years (2014-2020) as the state's most successful lifesaving development programme, then carried it personally into two more states, coordinating the inaugural SLSQ camp in 2019 and the inaugural SLSNSW camps in 2021 and 2022. Establishing the same member-development programme from scratch in three different states is a contribution directly and uniquely attributable to him.

In NSW he has also served in state emergency management roles at the Age and Open Championships (Deputy State Emergency Management Coordinator 2022/23; State Emergency Management Officer 2023/24), and his blended learning work was highly commended at the 2020 Australian Institute of Training & Development Excellence Awards. His peers have judged his service the best in the state across multiple domains: SLST Volunteer of the Year (2010/11), Lifesaver of the Year (2011/12) and Trainer of the Year twice (2011/12 and 2018). And the service continues: having moved interstate, he still serves Tasmania today on the SLST Operations Executive (2025-present). Two decades, three states, and counting.
EOF

Chris Jacobson's story is one of dedication that has never paused, from a young lifesaver joining Ulverstone SLSC in 2004 to one of the most influential volunteer leaders in modern Australian lifesaving. He stepped onto the national stage at the 2006 SLSA Youth Development Forum at the very start of his journey, and twenty years later he has never left it. By 2011/12 he was the SLSA Australian Surf Lifesaver of the Year, the youngest ever recipient and the only Tasmanian to receive the award. He went on to serve fourteen years on the Lifesaving Members Advisory Committee (2012-2025), and in 2016 became the youngest person to hold the role of National Chair of Lifesaving, which he held for nine years.

As National Chair he transformed how every Australian lifesaver is trained. He chaired the National Lifesaving Curriculum Review, chaired the rewrite of the Public Safety and Aquatic Rescue manual and delivered its first online interactive edition, chaired the redesign of the Bronze Medallion, Silver Medallion Aquatic Rescue and Silver Medallion Patrol Captain courses, and built the first nationally delivered blended learning model for the Surf Rescue Certificate and Bronze Medallion, work recognised with an international award for best use of blended learning in 2020. These reforms continue to shape the development of thousands of new members every year.

He has always looked to the movement's future. He founded the inaugural National Innovation Day, conceived and chaired the Expanding Horizons Review, now a core strategic project confronting the future volunteer and service delivery challenges facing the movement, and served as National Implementation Lead for Lifesaving CPR (2024-2026), the first nationally coordinated CPR quality improvement initiative implemented by a community first aid organisation in Australia. As Chair of the National Meritorious Awards Committee (2017-2024) he introduced the Youth Surf Life Saver of the Year award, ensuring the next generation is recognised as he once was.

Through all of it he has remained a frontline volunteer. He still patrols today at Elouera SLSC, remains a member and an asset to Ulverstone SLSC and Tasmania long after moving interstate, and gives so much of himself that members around the country routinely assume he is paid staff. He is not. He is a volunteer, and that is the measure of his dedication.
EOF

Chris joined Ulverstone SLSC in 2004 and has patrolled every season since, twenty-two unbroken years of frontline service that continues today at Elouera SLSC in Sydney. What makes his club service distinguished is not tenure alone but what he built along the way, and the fact that he has never really left. He remains a continuing member of Ulverstone and an ongoing asset to his home club long after moving interstate, still mentoring its members and still taking the phone call whenever the club needs advice or help with a project or a problem.

As Patrol Captain for nine consecutive seasons (2007-2016) he carried frontline rescue responsibility on Ulverstone's beach. As Vice President, Lifesaving (2011) and Club Training Officer (2011-2013) he built the club's lifesaving operations and education capability, and from 2007 he has served continuously as a Trainer, Assessor and Facilitator, delivering award courses that began at club level and grew to branch, state and national delivery. The training systems he later rebuilt for the whole country were first learned, tested and taught on his own club's beach, and the members he has trained and mentored across two decades are his most personal legacy.

His peers saw it early, naming him Club Person of the Year in 2010/11 and again in 2011/12, back-to-back recognition in consecutive seasons. Two decades on, the dedication has not dimmed. Chris remains the member every club officer knows they can call, at Ulverstone, at Elouera, and at clubs around the country.
EOF
cat > s9v3.txt <<'EOF'
Chris's state service tells a story few in the movement can match, and it spans three states. It begins in Tasmania, where he progressed from State Development Squad Captain (2005/06) and Under-19 Surf Life Saver of the Year (2007) through thirteen years on the State Emergency Response Team (2007-2020), the Awards of Excellence Panel (2009-2016), State Patrol Assessor (2010-2016) and State Duty Officer (2014-2020), to Chair of Lifesaving (2012-2016), the state's senior lifesaving position. As state Chair he authored Tasmania's Duty Officer training and standards and chaired the editorial panel that produced SLST's inaugural Standard Operating Procedures, documents the state's operations still stand on today.

His signature state contribution is the Lifesaving Development Camp. He coordinated Tasmania's inaugural camp and ran it for six years (2014-2020) as the state's most successful lifesaving development programme, then carried it personally into two more states, establishing the inaugural SLSQ camp in 2019 and the inaugural SLSNSW camps in 2021 and 2022. Building the same member development programme from scratch in three different states is a contribution directly and uniquely attributable to one person's dedication.

In NSW he has served in state emergency management roles at the Age and Open Championships, as Deputy State Emergency Management Coordinator in 2022/23 and State Emergency Management Officer in 2023/24, and his blended learning work was highly commended at the 2020 Australian Institute of Training and Development Excellence Awards. His peers have repeatedly judged his service the best in the state, naming him SLST Volunteer of the Year (2010/11), Lifesaver of the Year (2011/12) and Trainer of the Year twice (2011/12 and 2018).

Most telling of all is what happened after he left. Moving interstate usually ends a member's state service. Chris's never stopped. He continues to serve Tasmania today on the SLST Operations Executive (2025-present), still contributing to the state that shaped him years after he moved away. That is the pattern of his whole story, sustained dedication that outlasts geography. Two decades, three states, and counting.
EOF

Chris is known across SLSA as the person who moves the organisation forward, and his national record tells the story of a volunteer who kept showing up, kept innovating and kept lifting the standard for twenty years without pause. His service meets all three limbs of the Life Membership standard, with contributions that are unique and directly attributable to him rather than to any group he sat on.

Distinguished. The interpretive guidelines for this award cite the introduction of CPR as the benchmark example of a distinguished contribution. Chris was the National Implementation Lead for Lifesaving CPR (2024-2026), the first nationally coordinated CPR quality improvement initiative implemented by a community first aid organisation in Australia, personally leading the national roadshow that upskilled trainers around the country. That alone meets the benchmark, and it sits on top of a decade of national transformation. Appointed in 2016 as the youngest person to hold the role of National Chair of Lifesaving, he reshaped how every Australian lifesaver is trained. He chaired the 2019 National Lifesaving Curriculum Review, chaired the rewrite of the Public Safety and Aquatic Rescue manual and delivered its first online interactive edition, and chaired three national course redesigns across the Bronze Medallion, Silver Medallion Aquatic Rescue and Silver Medallion Patrol Captain. He built the first nationally delivered blended learning model for the Surf Rescue Certificate and Bronze Medallion, work whose quality was recognised beyond the movement with an international award for best use of blended learning in 2020 and a highly commended at the Australian Institute of Training and Development Excellence Awards. He founded and facilitated the inaugural National Innovation Day, and he conceived, founded and chaired the Expanding Horizons Review, which has become a core strategic project for the organisation, confronting the future volunteer and service delivery challenges facing the movement. Each of these initiatives exists because Chris saw the need, argued for it and carried it.

Significant. This is not the administration of an existing system but the transformation of it. Every Surf Rescue Certificate, Bronze Medallion and Silver Medallion candidate in Australia now trains through models and manuals Chris built or rebuilt, reforms that continue to shape the development of thousands of new members every year, and every club's resuscitation practice is being lifted by an initiative he led. Through twelve years on the National Meritorious Awards Committee (2013-2025), seven as Chair (2017-2024), he also shaped how SLSA recognises its own members, overseeing the Lifesaver of the Year and Volunteer of the Year awards and their judging panels, leading the 2021 review of the lifesaving award criteria and introducing the Youth Surf Life Saver of the Year award so that the next generation of standouts is recognised as he once was.

Sustained. His national service began at the 2006 SLSA Youth Development Forum, twenty years ago, and has never stopped. He has been a national Trainer, Assessor and Facilitator since 2007, piloted the Silver Medallion Aquatic Rescue in 2011, and served fourteen consecutive years on the Lifesaving Members Advisory Committee (2012-2025) with nine as National Chair. There is no gap in this record. Every season for two decades, Chris has been doing the work.

Conspicuous. He was named SLSA Australian Surf Lifesaver of the Year in 2011/12, the youngest ever recipient and the only Tasmanian recipient. His efforts have earned the praise of even his harshest critics, and the sheer volume and quality of his output is so far beyond what anyone expects of a volunteer that members around the country routinely assume he is paid staff. He is not, and never has been. Twenty years of that record, given freely, is the definition of conspicuous service.
EOF
